extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / educated early-18th-century readers interested in manners, morals, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Short, didactic periodical essays offering rules and observations about social conduct, manners, truthfulness, love, and public life—the kind of prose found in The Spectator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biting (the wit called a 'Bite')
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Biter' is one who thinks you a Fool, because you do not think him a Knave; a way of wit that depends upon deceit to make another appear ridiculous or be over-reach'd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics and examples: metaphor from beasts of prey (foxes to lambs); used by sharpers to overreach the unwary; adopted by shallow fops to dismiss or evade serious points in debate by crying 'Bite' to convert an earnest point into jest. Anti-patterns: using 'biting' to disown one's own nonsense, to evade force of reasonable argument, or to invent false particulars to impose upon credulity. Example anecdotes: the Yorkshire/apoplexy 'bite' and the condemned man negotiating his body then crying 'Bite, I am to be hang'd in Chains.' Footnote: Swift's description of the practice as a courtly refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about dreams and popular divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary dreams and popular arts of prediction (hand-lines, physiognomy, stars, entrails, birds, signatures) are uncertain, shadowy, and chimerical; placing weight on common dreams is superstitious and foolish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: do not lay stress upon ordinary dreams; only very extraordinary, exceptional revelations (rare cases) may be considered supernatural. Anti-patterns: treating stray occurrences or trivial signs as portents (e.g., straws, rusted iron), overinterpreting coincidences, or letting waking thoughts be wholly occupied by sleeping visions. The essay advocates rooting out popular errors about prophetic sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical 'qualifications' and business practices for a dream-interpreter (oneirocritick)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charismatic or pretended interpreters advertise peculiar credentials and fee structures to attract customers (e.g., having a second-sighted relative, bodily oddities, being born on the longest night, name quirks, lodgings where conjurers live).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial model and practices (satirized): interpret for the poor for free if their names are used as testimonials; interpret for people of quality by 'seeing their water'; assign a day for lovers; charge modest weekly fees for elderly women; provide rooms for those without conveniences. This entry should be read as a satirical catalogue of how charlatans legitimize themselves and monetize superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping love alive after marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Love after marriage requires active, ongoing effort: mutual endeavour to please, maintenance of decency and neatness, avoiding excessive familiarity, and preserving occasions for desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit prescriptions: avoid too great familiarity and laying aside common rules of decency (especially in dress); neatness and attentiveness preserve attraction; both parties should earnestly strive to please; a 'Man of Sense' (learning + business) helps keep conversation alive; occasional absences and occupations (engagement in business) supply the 'little absences' that preserve desire. Positive practices: complimenting and improving the partner's view of themselves (Erastus making Lætitia discover and praise her own qualities). Negative examples: Beaus who drop the 'bait' after marriage; Tom Tawdry, who provides no substance and provokes contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man of sense as preserve of conjugal esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: A man of sense is one acquainted with business and letters; his learning and employment make him more esteemed and interesting to his wife.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role: learning gives conversational resources that set men apart from 'common tattle' and supplies occasions for absence and agency that preserve attraction. Practical effect: engages the wife with new information and causes her to esteem him; lack of learning or business leads to contempt and loss of love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles against party-lying (truthfulness criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Party-lying—propagating systematic falsehoods in factional discourse—is morally reprehensible and not justified by shared participation or supposed good of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments/guidance: (1) Multiplicity of liars does not divide guilt—each participant bears full moral responsibility; (2) Diffusion among many may reduce shame but not guilt—preferring reputation over real virtue is hypocrisy; (3) Purported service to a cause cannot justify lying—truth must be spoken even at personal cost. Practical rule: do not accept lies merely because they are fashionable or serve factional ends; treat party-stories skeptically. Quoted ideal: one should prefer truth even at personal loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness and proper conduct in clubs and company (against petty 'tyrants')
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who take offices in clubs (proveditor, organizer) should serve the felicity of the company rather than impose unalterable edicts; the 'tyrant' who turns minor offices into absolute dominion is oppressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected behaviour: officers should recommend with willingness to debate and submit, not issue unalterable commands about trivial matters (what to eat, where to sit, when to change tavern); they should not interrupt or control all conversation according to humours. Remedies suggested: collective resistance, exposing and dethroning the usurper by calculated social sanctions (satirical threat of letting him taste a dinner he did not order). Example: 'Dionysius' who escalates from helpful steward to intolerable controller of the group's liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating women in conversation: genuine respect vs. coxcombry
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-bred men converse with women with respect that flows from heart and understanding (not empty professions); they avoid troublesome over-complaisance or rude contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive standard: gentle, sincere civility and deference—treat a visiting woman 'as gently as their sisters' and avoid offensive suppositions. Anti-patterns: the familiar coxcomb who contradicts on every occasion, calls a woman a liar, or uses faux-imitations of good breeding that become rude or banishing. Social remedy: public reprimand, leaving the company if maltreated, or appealing to published maxims of behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators and practice of thrift (private and public)
rubrics_metrics.description: A thriving frugal man shows regularity and simplicity in expense, dress, servants, and house; public spaces (e.g., the Royal Exchange) should be kept respectable to encourage commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs to evaluate thrift: visible simplicity and order in personal expenditure and public comportment. Civic implication: neglect and infiltration of disreputable vendors and beggars into commercial walks degrade the place and discourage merchants, which signals civic decline. Practical prescription: restore ancient economy and simple manners; keep public marketplaces clear of ragamuffins so men of consequence will frequent them.
